steps.action:
The lighthouse at Blackthorn Point only ever showed one color to the world: a hard, white eye that swept the horizon every twelve seconds. To the ships that passed in the night, it was a warning and a promise. To Arlen Grey, who lived within its cold stone ribs, it was a metronome that split his days into equal, measured lengths.

Every twelve seconds, a soft, mechanical sigh of the turning lens.

Every twelve seconds, a streak of light over an empty sea.

Arlen had been the keeper for twenty-one years. Before him, his father had tended the lamp, and before his father, an uncle whose photograph still hung, smoke-faded, in the narrow kitchen. The lighthouse was a family inheritance in the way some families passed down rings or curses. It stood three miles from the nearest village, reached by a road that turned to mud whenever the sky so much as considered rain.

In the mornings, he woke before dawn, even on the days he did not need to. Habit had become a second spine; it held him more rigidly than bone. He rose, pulled on his wool sweater with its elbow patches worn pale, and climbed the spiral steps to extinguish the lamp before the first gray hints of daylight shouldered the dark aside.

The lamp itself was modern now, electric and obedient, not like the old oil light he’d known as a boy. But the rest of the tower clung to the past the way salt clung to the windows. Stone worn smooth by generations of boots. Brass rails polished by absent fingers. A narrow bed. A table. A radio. Shelves of logbooks with thin black handwriting marching across their pages, all the way back to 1894 when the first Grey had written, in a satisfying ink flourish, “Light Lit. Weather: Clear. Sea: Calm.”

Arlen kept his own log with the same seriousness, though no one ever read it but him. The Coast Guard had tablets and satellites now. They could watch the sea from offices that never smelled of mildew or kerosene. But every day, at noon, Arlen sat at the table, uncapped his pen, and recorded:

Date. Time. Weather. Visibility. Any passing ships.

Sometimes he noted other things, slipping past the practical lines like an extra wave after the regular set.

“Gulls louder than yesterday.”

“Dreamed of snow, woke to fog.”

“Whale’s breath spotted at 03:12. Sounded like an old man sighing.”

He did not know why he wrote those parts. Perhaps because writing them down made them feel less like the inventions of a lonely mind and more like facts.

Twice a month, he drove into the village in a rusted truck that always seemed surprised to start. He bought supplies—flour, coffee, tinned tomatoes, lamp cleaner, batteries—and listened to whatever gossip the butcher or the postmistress offered him. They were kind, in the distracted way people are kind to human landmarks. “How’s the light, Arlen?” they would ask, as if checking on a retired relative. “Still shining?”

“Still shining,” he would reply.

He had once been married, briefly, in a thick August when the nights were short and full of insects. Maeve had lasted fifteen months before deciding that the rhythm of the tower did not match the rhythm of her heart. “It’s not the isolation,” she’d told him, packing her red coat into a duffel. “I could survive the quiet. It’s the sameness, Arlen. Every day here is like a photograph of the day before. I need something that moves.”

He had almost said, “The beam moves,” but bit his tongue. Maeve’s hair had smelled of oranges; when she kissed him goodbye, the citrus ghost followed him up the steps for weeks.

After she left, the lighthouse grew larger around him, as if some invisible scaffolding had been removed. He noticed the drips in the ceiling on rainy nights, the way the wind found new ways to whistle through the cracked caulking of the windowframes. He noticed, more than anything, the space in the kitchen where a second chair was no longer necessary.

Now, at forty-nine, Arlen could not imagine a different life, although he sometimes tried. He would picture himself working at the hardware store in the village, or fixing engines in the mechanic’s yard. In these daydreams, he had colleagues, people who said his name so often the sound of it lost its weight. In those lives, there were perhaps dinners that were not eaten alone.

But he did not leave. The light needed watching, and he had been born into the watching of it. The ships did not know his name, but they knew his work.

On an evening in late November, the sea turned thick and black and whispered of snow inland. The wind had been steady out of the north all day, stripping the last of the leaves off the scrub trees along the cliff. Standing on the iron platform that circled the lamp room, Arlen could smell the promise of a hard freeze. He checked the bolts on the railing, feeling the metal bite through his gloves, then went back inside to make his rounds.

He listened to the marine forecast on the radio: gale warning, visibility decreasing, temperatures dropping. The weatherman’s voice was soft with rehearsed concern. “Mariners are advised to remain in port where possible.”

Arlen sipped his coffee and glanced at the logbook, where that morning he had written: “Sky like dirty wool. Sea restless. Bad feeling in the tide.”

He was not superstitious. But the ocean was a presence to him, and like any old neighbor, it had moods.

The snow began after nightfall, flurries at first, then impatient, slanting sheets. It turned the world outside the narrow windows into an abstract of motion and whiteness. The beam lifted and swept, turning the falling snow into a tunnel of brightness every twelve seconds.

He checked the generators, the backup batteries, the radio. He walked his circle through the tower as he did on storm nights: lamp room, observation room, stairs, door to the outside, kitchen, radio, lamp room again. He tightened his sweater around himself and listened to the wind pick up layers like a choir adding voices.

It was near midnight when the first call came through.

“Blackthorn Light, Blackthorn Light, this is fishing vessel Maribel Rose, do you copy?” The voice on Channel 16 crackled with static and strain. “We are—uh—we are experiencing navigation issues, repeat, we have equipment failure. Requesting guidance, over.”

Arlen turned the volume up and leaned toward the radio as if proximity could clear the signal.

“Maribel Rose, this is Blackthorn Light, reading you. State your position, over.”

Silence hissed back at him. Then, after a moment: “We’re—our GPS is… we’re not sure. We were running south, about fifteen miles offshore, but we’ve lost chart plotter and radar. We can see your light intermittently through the snow. Feels like we’re being pushed closer to shore. Engines are fighting the swell. Visibility near zero. Requesting bearing to safe water, over.”

He pictured them: a trawler maybe, heavy with gear, three or four men in orange slickers, faces raw with cold, trying to parse a world that had turned to white noise.

“Maribel Rose, what is your compass heading and speed, over?”

There was a pause; a different voice came on, rougher, impatient.

“Heading three-one-zero, speed five knots, but we’re slipping. Feels like we’re drifting east. We can’t see a damn thing, Blackthorn. Just your light smearing through the snow. Feels like it’s everywhere and nowhere. Over.”

Arlen stood, one hand braced on the radio table, listening as the wind clawed at the tower. He opened the drawer below, pulled out his paper charts, a pencil, and his old brass dividers. Electronics failed; ink did not.

“Maribel Rose, what was your last confirmed position before equipment failure? Over.”

“Uh—” Paper crackled over the channel, voices muttered. “Half an hour ago, position was five-four degrees, one-nine minutes north; zero-two degrees, three-six minutes west. Over.”

Arlen’s pencil moved. He marked their point, plotted their heading and distance in the time since, subtracting for probable drift, wind direction, the set of the current he had watched all his life. Numbers became lines, lines became a ghost of a boat feeling its way blind toward rock.

The waters off Blackthorn Point were treacherous. Under the surface lay a ragged spine of stone, sharp and indifferent. In summer, when the sea was calm and amused, you could see the swell break white over the hidden teeth. In winter, those teeth waited invisibly.

He pressed his pencil hard enough to tear the thin, blue-ruled paper.

“Maribel Rose, this is Blackthorn Light.” His voice, when he heard it in the cramped room, sounded like someone else’s: calm, authoritative, assured. “By my reckoning, if you maintain present heading and speed, you risk grounding on Blackthorn Shoals within forty minutes. Recommend you alter course to heading one-eight-zero, increase speed to seven knots if able. That will take you back toward deeper water, away from shore. Confirm you can comply, over.”

The radio hummed. Then: “One-eight-zero, seven knots.” The rough voice again, doubt threaded through the words. “You certain of that, Blackthorn? We can barely hold five in this—feels like we’re being pushed sideways. Over.”

Arlen looked up through the narrow window toward where he knew the Maribel Rose might be: somewhere out there in the dark, his light painting the snow that swallowed them. He thought of the mathematics in his head, the currents he knew like the back of his hand, the way the tide wrapped around the point, the wind clawing from the north.

“I am certain,” he said. “But you must trust your compass, not your eyes. Head one-eight-zero. If you can’t make seven knots, make as much as you safely can. I’m increasing the lamp’s intensity if possible. Keep me updated on your heading and any sight of land or changes in swell. Over.”

He went up to the lamp room, phone clipped to his belt, and made the adjustments. The lamp hummed a little brighter. The mechanism had safety limits—it could not turn night to noon—but he knew enough leeway to push the bulb slightly hotter without burning it out. The beam thickened, throwing a stronger arm through the storm.

The next half hour stretched. The tower groaned under the wind’s weight. Snow hammered the glass like fingers. Arlen divided his time between the radio and the windows, eyes searching the blackness for any sign: a weak deck light, a sliver of mast, a shape where no shape should be.

“Blackthorn, this is Maribel Rose,” came through, faint but there. “Adjusted to one-eight-zero. Speed fluctuating between four and six knots. Seas rough. Feels like we’re riding up and falling into holes. No sight of land. Over.”

Arlen did his math again, making small corrections. “Hold that heading. You should begin to feel swell lengthen as you move into deeper water. Listen for the surf—if you hear breaking waves, you are too close to shore. Over.”

“Copy. Over.”

They fell into a grim rhythm, like a call-and-response hymn.

“Heading check. Over.”

“One-eight-zero, Blackthorn. Over.”

“Any change in swell? Over.”

“Maybe. Hard to tell. Over.”

“Keep me informed. Over.”

At 00:47, the rough voice came back, a note of something like hope in it. “Swell feels different, Blackthorn. Not as steep. Still can’t see more than thirty, forty yards. But it doesn’t feel like we’re climbing cliffs anymore. Over.”

Arlen allowed himself to breathe a fraction deeper. “That’s a good sign, Maribel Rose. Hold heading another ten minutes, then come to one-seven-zero to clear an offshore shoal belt. That will carry you south into open water. Over.”

“Copy. Coming to one-seven-zero in ten. Over.”

He went back to the lamp room, hand on the glass, looking out at a world that remained featureless. Somewhere inside that howling blankness, men were wrestling machinery and fear. His fear stayed quiet, caged behind decades of habit. There was nothing else he could do but talk them along the line he’d drawn on paper.

At 01:09, the radio crackled again.

“Blackthorn Light, this is Coast Guard Cutter Huxley. We are inbound to intercept Maribel Rose, homing on your light. Estimate your tower bearing from our present position as zero-four-five, range eight nautical miles. Confirm your operational status and any known hazards in our approach. Over.”

Arlen glanced at the logbook, at the radio clock. He pictured them triangulating with far better tools than his pencil and charts.

“Cutter Huxley, this is Blackthorn Light. Operational and fully functional. Hazards on your approach: Blackthorn Shoals extending two-point-five nautical miles northeast from point, drying rocks visible at low tide. Recommend you favor eastern approach, staying outside the two-hundred-foot contour line. Maribel Rose is currently heading one-seven-zero, estimated six nautical miles south-southeast of my position, moving toward safer water. Over.”

“Copy all, Blackthorn. Appreciate the local knowledge. Over.”

There was something in the Coast Guard officer’s tone—respect, perhaps, or simply relief at having a fixed point in the chaos—that warmed the cold room a degree.

Thirty minutes later, the Maribel Rose called again. The background noise had changed. Arlen could hear more engine, less sea.

“Blackthorn, this is Maribel Rose. Swell’s longer now, like you said. Having to throttle back; waves starting to come from the quarter instead of the bow. But we ain’t hearing any breakers. No sight of land. Over.”

Arlen closed his eyes, seeing their path on the chart overlaying the reality outside. “That’s the offshore swell. You’re clear of the shoals. In ten minutes, come to heading one-five-zero. That will set you on a course away from Blackthorn Point and into deeper, more uniform water. Coast Guard Cutter Huxley is en route to your position from northeast; switch to Channel 06 after course change for direct comms with them. Over.”

There was a hollered exchange on their end, then the rough voice came back, softened.

“Blackthorn… we do as you say, that’s it, yeah? We’re out? Over.”

“You’ll be out of the worst of it,” Arlen said. “The rest is seamanship and patience. But you’re past the teeth. Over.”

Silence, then: “Copy that. Changing to one-five-zero in ten, then over to six. Thank you, Blackthorn. Over.”

He could have answered many things. Instead he said, simply: “Stand by. Over.”

At 02:02, Cutter Huxley checked back in briefly, their voice crisp and professional despite the hour.

“Blackthorn Light, Huxley. We have Maribel Rose on radar and visual at close range. Sea state remains rough but improving. All souls accounted for. We’re escorting them south to calmer waters. Appreciate your assistance tonight. Over.”

Arlen looked around at the empty tower. The lamp turned. The snow had thinned to feathers. Somewhere out there, two vessels rode the swell, one large and gray, one smaller and tired, both held in the residual glow of his lamp’s long arc.

“Glad to hear it, Huxley. Safe passage. Blackthorn standing by. Out.”

He logged it, his pen moving slowly.

“00:11 – Mayday-equivalent call from FV Maribel Rose. Lost electronics, low visibility, risk of grounding. Provided bearings and course adjustments via manual calculations. 01:35 – USCGC Huxley inbound; coordinated approach. 02:02 – Maribel Rose confirmed safe, escorted south. Storm abating.”

He hesitated, then added beneath, in smaller letters:

“Felt the sea’s anger like an old story retold. Light did its work. So did I.”

When dawn finally bled into the sky, it came pale and exhausted. The snow stopped. The world outside his windows reassembled itself: the dark smear of the horizon, the jagged, black rocks below, crusted white with foam. The wind fell to a mutter. The sea, as if ashamed of the night’s tantrum, smoothed out by degrees.

Arlen climbed to the lamp room at the appointed time and clicked the lamp off. The light’s sudden absence felt like a held breath released.

He stepped out onto the encircling platform. The metal was slick beneath his boots. Cold bit his cheeks, his nose, his fingertips through the gloves. He leaned on the railing and looked, squinting, toward the south. There, far off, two specks moved along the horizon, barely distinguishable: a larger one, squared-off, and a smaller one, trailing.

They were too far to see him. But he raised a hand anyway, an unconscious gesture, half-wave, half-blessing.

The tower was very quiet when he went back inside. Without the lamp’s hum and the storm’s roar, its age pressed in on him. He brewed coffee, listening to the unremarkable drip and hiss. On the kitchen wall, the photo of his uncle glowered down in sepia, as if suspicious of all these modern intrusions—radios and generators and Coast Guard cutters.

Arlen set his mug down, wiped a ring of coffee from the table, and opened the back of the old wooden clock that hung above the logbooks. Inside, nested among dust and two long-dead spiders, lay a bundle of letters, tied with thin blue cord. They belonged to his father: creased envelopes from ships’ captains and fishermen, written in careful or clumsy hands, thanking the light for this or that narrow escape.

He had read them many times. Some were terse, just a line or two. Others rambled, describing waves “as high as houses,” or children born nine months after a storm that had nearly claimed their fathers. Each letter, in its own way, tried to give shape to gratitude for something they could not quite name.

Arlen loosened the cord and slid last night’s log page among them. It did not belong, strictly speaking. The men of the Maribel Rose would not write. They did not need to, and he did not expect it. Still, he felt that what had happened in the small hours belonged with these other tales of the line between disaster and its absence.

He retied the cord and closed the clock.

At noon, he took his truck into the village. The road was treacherous with new snow over old ice, but he knew its curves like his own thoughts. Patches of sunlight skated between clouds, turning the frozen puddles into quicksilver. The village, when he reached it, wore its winter face: chimneys coughing smoke, children in padded coats kicking at slush, the harbor a forest of bare masts.
